newsitem.title: UK: Thames warns on tax as yr profits rise.
newsitem.headline: Thames warns on tax as yr profits rise.

text.p: Year profits at British water and sewerage company Thames Water Plc surged on Tuesday, as expected, as it promised to seek a mandate for a return of cash to shareholders, limiting share price falls as the overall market eased.

The company, which supplies London with water, resigned itself to paying a tax on "excess profits" planned by the new Labour government but warned that the levy could damage investment if it is too severe.

Thames said in a statement that pretax profits before exceptional items jumped 19 percent to 384 million pounds ($628.3 million) and paid out a total dividend of 34.3 pence per share, up 22 percent partly as a result of a 10 percent share buyback last year.
"They've come out with a pretty good set of figures and the market seems to like the look of them," one trader said.
"But now it's a question of waiting to see what kind of tax they get hit with, so (shares) won't go too high," he added.
Thames' results coincided with a warning from industry regulator Ofwat not to undermine investment by paying out hefty dividends in a statement to mark publication of its annual report.
"I am...concerned that companies should fulfil their investment programmes and that unjustifiably high dividend increases do not undermine that," Ofwat head Ian Byatt said.
Thames shares touched a high of 682 pence but later eased back to close down one pence at 670 pence as the overall market closed down 62.9 points at 4,682.2.

Managing director Bill Alexander told Reuters that the company would seek a mandate from shareholders at its annual meeting for a buyback of shares after spending 226 million pounds on a similar move last year.

He said the company was resigned to paying a one-off tax on excess profits proposed by the new Labour government to fund a three billion pound programme to cut unemployment, which will be a central plank of the administration's first budget on July 2.
"I don't think there's any way with the mandate the government got...that we're going to avoid it," he said.

But he added that Thames wanted to "make sure the tax is a fair and appropriate one," and warned that if the levy were too severe, "it'll damage our investment programme and that's creating jobs directly in the south east (of England)."

The centre-left Labour government swept to power with a landslide victory in a general election on May 1 and has vowed to introduce the "windfall" tax on privatised utilities although few details have been released.
Alexander said it was too early to make provisions for the tax but said that a strong balance sheet should mean "we should be able to cope with it."
"The government are determined to give the industry a bloody nose, we'll just have to wipe our face and get on with it," he said.

Utilities such as water and electricity companies which were privatised under the previous Conservative government have come under fierce criticism from Labour and consumer lobby groups for hefty shareholder payouts and chunky executive pay packets.

Water companies have drawn further fire for allowing nearly 800 million gallons of supplies to seep out of pipes daily as some firms have curbed non-essential domestic use during the country's current drought, the worst for 200 years.
Thames has one of the worst records on leakage in the country but has now cut its rate to 28 percent from 39 percent in 1995/96.
It aims to reduce this figure to 14 percent by 2000, Alexander said.
The government has set up a 10-point plan for water companies, including mandatory targets to cut leakage, in an attempt to ensure the country copes with the drought.
Thames warned that if there were not significant amounts of rain in the next few weeks, it would become more difficult to avoid restrictions in its area.
The company said it should maintain real dividend growth and that new businesses are expected to produce a strong earnings stream.
"The market is more confident about its international portfolio and Thames seems to be delivering on the dividend," said one analyst who asked not to be named.
Alexander said that although payouts were unlikely to match last year's 22 percent rise, "we'll be paying reasonable dividend going forward."

Thames said its ability to increase the dividend was also a result of a strong contribution from non-regulated business including international operations, which contributed 26 million pounds to profits and should see a strengthening earnings stream.
"We'd like to be able to contribute about 10 percent of our profits from our non-core activities...by the year 2000," Alexander said.
($ = 0.611 British Pounds)
